questions.question: What is the output of the query `SELECT INSTR('Database', 'a');` in standard SQL?
questions.title: `SELECT INSTR('Database', 'a');`

sections.label: Steps
sections.content: INSTR returns the 1-based position of the first occurrence of a substring. In "Database": D(1) a(2) t(3) a(4) b(5) a(6) s(7) e(8). The first 'a' occurs at position **2**.

questions.question: When utilizing standard SQL window functions, how does the behavior of the ROW_NUMBER() function definitively contrast with that of the DENSE_RANK() function when evaluating completely identical values within a designated data partition?
questions.title: ROW_NUMBER() vs DENSE_RANK() on identical values
options: Both give tied rows identical values
ROW_NUMBER gives tied rows the same number; DENSE_RANK gives unique numbers
ROW_NUMBER gives tied rows unique numbers; DENSE_RANK gives them the same rank
questions.answer: ROW_NUMBER gives tied rows unique numbers; DENSE_RANK gives them the same rank

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: For tied (identical) values within a partition, **ROW_NUMBER() still assigns a unique, sequential number to every row (no ties — order among equal values is arbitrary)**, whereas **DENSE_RANK() assigns the same rank to all tied rows and continues the next rank without any gap** (e.g., ranks 1,1,2 instead of 1,2,3).

questions.question: Which SQL command is used to update index statistics to help the Query Optimizer make better execution plans?

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **`ANALYZE`** (e.g., `ANALYZE TABLE` in MySQL) or **`UPDATE STATISTICS`** (SQL Server) refreshes the statistics the query optimizer uses to choose efficient execution plans.

questions.question: Which query retrieves the second highest salary from the "Employees" table?

options: SELECT Salary FROM Employees ORDER BY Salary LIMIT 2;
SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees);
SELECT MIN(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE Salary > (SELECT MIN(Salary) FROM Employees);
SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE Salary = (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees);
questions.answer: SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees);

sections.label: Answer
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees
WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees);
```
**Logic:** Find the maximum salary strictly less than the overall maximum — that is by definition the second-highest value.

questions.question: Which aggregate function is typically used to find the lowest value in a specific column?
questions.title: Aggregate function for the lowest value

sections.label: Answer

questions.question: How does the explicit definition of an INSTEAD OF trigger functionally alter the default behavioral response of a relational database engine when a standard INSERT modification operation is executed against an underlying view?
questions.title: INSTEAD OF trigger on a view — behavior change
options: The insert runs first and the trigger runs afterwards
The insert is converted into an update automatically
All inserts into the view are blocked permanently
The trigger's code runs instead of the insert
questions.answer: The trigger's code runs instead of the insert

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: An INSTEAD OF trigger **completely replaces the database's default INSERT action on the view** — instead of the engine attempting to insert directly into the view's base table(s), the code inside the trigger runs instead, giving the developer full control over how (or whether) the underlying tables are actually modified.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the CROSS APPLY or LATERAL join operator?
questions.title: Purpose of CROSS APPLY / LATERAL
options: Combine two result sets and remove duplicates
Join tables on equal keys only
Build a Cartesian product with no correlation
Let the right-side expression reference columns of each left-side row
questions.answer: Let the right-side expression reference columns of each left-side row

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: CROSS APPLY (SQL Server) / LATERAL (standard SQL/PostgreSQL) allows a **table-valued expression on the right side to reference columns from the table on the left side of the join** — useful for joining a table to a table-valued function or a correlated subquery per row, something a regular JOIN cannot do.

questions.question: What happens if you execute a DELETE statement without a WHERE clause?
questions.title: DELETE without a WHERE clause
options: All rows are deleted but the table structure remains
Only the first row is deleted
questions.answer: All rows are deleted but the table structure remains

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: It **deletes every row in the table** (but keeps the table structure/schema intact, unlike TRUNCATE/DROP) — this operation is logged row-by-row and can be rolled back within a transaction.

questions.question: What is the fundamental logical reason why an index created on a VARCHAR column will generally NOT be utilized by the database query optimizer when a formulated query contains the filtering predicate WHERE ColumnName LIKE '%pattern'?
questions.title: Why an index on VARCHAR isn't used for `LIKE '%pattern'`
options: Indexes work only for numeric comparisons
A leading wildcard gives no fixed prefix, so the sorted index cannot be searched
questions.answer: A leading wildcard gives no fixed prefix, so the sorted index cannot be searched

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Because a **leading wildcard (%) means the search pattern doesn't start with a known prefix**, so the optimizer cannot use the index's sorted structure (typically a B-tree, ordered left-to-right by prefix) to narrow the search — it must scan every row instead. (An index CAN still be used for `LIKE 'pattern%'`, where the wildcard is only at the end.)

sections.content: **`WITH`** (e.g., `WITH cte_name AS (SELECT ...)`).

questions.title: Command to permanently save transaction changes
questions.answer: COMMIT

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **`COMMIT`**.

questions.question: Which query displays the current system date and time in MySQL or SQL Server?
questions.title: Query for current system date/time
options: SELECT NOW(); (MySQL) or SELECT GETDATE(); (SQL Server)
questions.answer: SELECT NOW(); (MySQL) or SELECT GETDATE(); (SQL Server)

sections.content: **`SELECT NOW();`** (MySQL) or **`SELECT GETDATE();`** (SQL Server).

questions.question: In the critical context of database transaction logs, the Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) protocol strictly mandates that a specific sequence of physical storage events occurs before a transaction is formally designated as fully committed. What is this mandate?
questions.title: WAL mandate before commit
options: Only the commit record is needed, not the changes
Data pages must be written to disk before the log
Locks must be released before anything is logged
The log records, including the commit record, must reach stable storage before the commit is acknowledged
questions.answer: The log records, including the commit record, must reach stable storage before the commit is acknowledged

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: WAL mandates that **all log records describing a transaction's changes (including its commit record) must be written to stable/durable storage before the transaction is acknowledged as committed** — ensuring the changes can always be redone/recovered even if a crash occurs immediately after.

questions.question: Consider a complex scenario where a correlated subquery returns a dataset containing NULL values. If an outer query utilizes the NOT IN operator to filter against this specific subquery, what will be the definitive resulting execution behavior?
questions.title: NOT IN against a subquery containing NULL
options: Only rows with NULL values are returned
questions.answer: No rows are returned

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: If the subquery result set contains even one NULL, the entire `NOT IN` comparison **returns an empty result set (no rows at all)** — because comparing any value to NULL yields UNKNOWN, and `NOT IN` requires all comparisons to definitively evaluate to true, which becomes impossible once a NULL is involved.

questions.title: Query to count distinct departments

questions.question: In the context of window functions, what is the difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK() when encountering tied values?
questions.title: RANK() vs DENSE_RANK() on ties
options: DENSE_RANK leaves gaps after ties; RANK does not
RANK leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK does not
questions.answer: RANK leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK does not

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **RANK() leaves a gap after ties** — if two rows tie for rank 1, the next row gets rank 3 (skipping 2). **DENSE_RANK() leaves no gap** — the next row after a tie at rank 1 gets rank 2.

questions.question: Which operation transforms row-level data into columnar format (cross-tabulation)?
questions.title: Operation converting rows into columns (cross-tabulation)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **PIVOT** transforms row-level data into columnar format for cross-tabulation-style reporting.

questions.question: Which window function allows you to access data from a subsequent row (a row that comes after the current row) in the same result set without using a self-join?
questions.title: Window function to access a subsequent row
questions.answer: LEAD()

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **`LEAD()`** returns a value from a following row in the result set (the counterpart, `LAG()`, accesses a preceding row) — both work without needing a self-join.

questions.title: `SELECT ROUND(123.456, 1);`

questions.question: What is the distinguishing functional purpose of a recursive Common Table Expression (CTE) when directly comparing it to a standard, non-recursive CTE within modern relational database query formulation architectures?
questions.title: Recursive CTE vs non-recursive CTE
options: It references itself, so it can walk hierarchical data
It stores its result permanently in a table
It can be used only in INSERT statements
It runs faster because its results are cached
questions.answer: It references itself, so it can walk hierarchical data

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A recursive CTE **references itself within its own definition**, allowing it to repeatedly process and build upon its own previous result set — used for hierarchical/tree-structured data (e.g., org charts, bill-of-materials) — whereas a non-recursive CTE is just a named, reusable single-pass query result.

questions.question: When architecting a materialized view for performance, what specific characteristic must all underlying aggregate functions and calculated expressions inherently possess to guarantee that the database engine can successfully generate an index?
questions.title: Materialized view — requirement for aggregates to be indexable
options: Dependent on the current system time
questions.answer: Deterministic

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: All aggregate functions and calculated expressions used in an indexed/materialized view must be **deterministic** (they must always return the same result for the same input values) — non-deterministic expressions (like functions depending on current time) cannot be indexed, since the index must reflect stable, reproducible values.

questions.question: Which logical operator reverses the truth value of a boolean expression?
questions.title: Logical operator reversing a boolean's truth value
questions.answer: NOT

questions.question: If two transactions attempt to update the same row simultaneously, which concurrency model relies on row versioning to detect conflicts at commit time rather than locking the row immediately?
questions.title: Concurrency model using row versioning instead of locking
questions.answer: Optimistic concurrency control (MVCC)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)**, often implemented via **MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)** — it lets transactions proceed without locking and checks for conflicts (using row versions/timestamps) only at commit time.

questions.question: Which specific aggregate expansion clause within the GROUP BY statement mathematically commands the query engine to generate a comprehensive result set encompassing every possible permutation of subtotals across the specified dimension columns?
questions.title: GROUP BY clause generating all subtotal permutations
questions.answer: GROUP BY CUBE(...)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **`GROUP BY CUBE(...)`** generates subtotals for every possible combination of the specified grouping columns, including the grand total (a related but less exhaustive option is `ROLLUP`, which generates only a hierarchical subset of subtotals).

questions.question: If a composite primary key constraint is explicitly defined utilizing both Columns A and B, which of the following statements accurately reflects the fundamental referential integrity rules governing any associated downstream foreign key constraints?
questions.title: Composite primary key (A, B) — foreign key implications
options: A foreign key must reference both A and B together
Foreign keys cannot reference a composite key
A foreign key may reference only column A
A foreign key may reference only column B
questions.answer: A foreign key must reference both A and B together

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Any foreign key referencing this composite primary key **must reference both columns A and B together as a pair** (a composite foreign key) — a foreign key cannot reference just one column of a composite primary key; referential integrity is enforced on the full combination.

questions.question: When querying hierarchical data (like an employee-manager relationship in the same table), which type of join is primarily required?
questions.title: Join type for hierarchical (employee-manager) data in the same table
options: Natural join with a different table
Full outer join with a second table
questions.answer: Self join

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **self-join** (typically an outer join of the table to itself, joining EmployeeID to ManagerID) is required to relate each employee row to their manager's row within the same table.

questions.question: What is the result of the query `SELECT 1 = 1 AND NULL = NULL;` in standard SQL?
questions.title: `SELECT 1 = 1 AND NULL = NULL;`
questions.answer: NULL

sections.label: Steps
sections.content: `1 = 1` → TRUE. `NULL = NULL` → UNKNOWN (NULL), because SQL's three-valued logic never treats NULL as equal to anything, including itself. `TRUE AND UNKNOWN` → UNKNOWN (NULL).

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: NULL (Unknown)

questions.question: How does the EXISTS operator evaluate a subquery compared to the IN operator?
questions.title: EXISTS vs IN — subquery evaluation
options: EXISTS requires the subquery to return NULL
EXISTS only checks whether any row is returned; IN compares against the returned values
IN only checks whether any row exists; EXISTS compares values
questions.answer: EXISTS only checks whether any row is returned; IN compares against the returned values

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: `EXISTS` checks **only whether the subquery returns any rows at all** (a boolean existence check, stopping at the first match — doesn't care about actual row values), while `IN` **compares the outer value against the full list of values returned by the subquery**, evaluating actual value matches.

questions.question: In standard SQL query execution order, which of the following accurately represents the strict logical processing sequence that the database engine adheres to when evaluating a standard SELECT statement containing aggregation functions?
questions.title: Standard SQL logical processing order (with aggregation)
options: FROM → SELECT → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY
WHERE → FROM → GROUP BY → SELECT → HAVING → ORDER BY
SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
questions.answer: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY

sections.label: Answer
sections.content:
The logical order is:
**FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY** (LIMIT/OFFSET last) — note this differs from the order you *write* the clauses in the query.

questions.question: Which normal form is strictly violated if a table contains a transitive dependency?
questions.title: Normal form violated by transitive dependency
questions.answer: Third Normal Form (3NF)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Third Normal Form (3NF)** is violated by a transitive dependency (a non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute rather than directly on the key).

questions.question: Under the strict SQL standard definitions, which specific database concurrency phenomenon is successfully prevented by the "REPEATABLE READ" transaction isolation level, but remains theoretically possible until the isolation is escalated to "SERIALIZABLE"?
questions.title: REPEATABLE READ prevents ___ but not until SERIALIZABLE
questions.answer: Phantom reads

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Phantom reads.** REPEATABLE READ stops dirty reads and non-repeatable reads, but phantom rows (new rows matching a range query) can still appear. Only SERIALIZABLE prevents them.

questions.question: What is the precise functional processing difference between the CROSS JOIN operator and the CROSS APPLY operator when specifically dealing with Table-Valued Functions (TVFs) in advanced multi-table SQL querying?
questions.title: CROSS JOIN vs CROSS APPLY with Table-Valued Functions
options: CROSS APPLY can pass each left row's columns into a TVF; CROSS JOIN cannot
CROSS JOIN can pass left columns into a TVF; CROSS APPLY cannot
CROSS APPLY returns unmatched rows; CROSS JOIN does not
questions.answer: CROSS APPLY can pass each left row's columns into a TVF; CROSS JOIN cannot

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: `CROSS JOIN` requires the joined table/expression to be **independent of the left table** (no row-by-row correlation), so it cannot be used with a TVF that takes a column from the left table as a parameter. `CROSS APPLY` **can invoke the TVF once per row of the left table, passing that row's column values as arguments**, enabling row-level correlated calls that CROSS JOIN cannot express.

SELECT DISTINCT Department, COUNT(Department) FROM Employees ORDER BY Department;
SELECT Department, SUM(*) FROM Employees GROUP BY Department;
questions.answer: SELECT Department, COUNT(*) FROM Employees GROUP BY Department;

sections.label: Answer

questions.question: Which of the following precisely describes the architectural data layout difference between a Clustered Index and a Non-Clustered Index within a standard relational database physical storage engine?
questions.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index — data layout
options: A table may have many clustered indexes but only one non-clustered
A non-clustered index orders the table rows; a clustered index is a separate structure
A clustered index orders the table rows themselves; a non-clustered index is a separate structure with pointers
questions.answer: A clustered index orders the table rows themselves; a non-clustered index is a separate structure with pointers

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Clustered Index physically sorts and stores the actual table data rows in the order of the index key** (there can be only one per table, since data can only be physically ordered one way). A **Non-Clustered Index is a separate structure that stores the key values plus pointers back to the actual data rows**, leaving the base table's physical order untouched (a table can have many non-clustered indexes).

questions.question: What is a "Deadlock" in database concurrency control?
questions.title: What is a Deadlock (in DB concurrency)
options: A transaction is rolled back automatically
A table is dropped while still in use
A query runs without an index
Transactions wait on each other's locks in a cycle, so none can proceed
questions.answer: Transactions wait on each other's locks in a cycle, so none can proceed

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A deadlock is a situation where **two or more transactions are each waiting for a lock held by the other(s), forming a cycle of dependencies**, so none of them can ever proceed — the DBMS typically detects this and forcibly aborts (rolls back) one transaction to break the cycle.

questions.question: Which function returns the number of characters in a string expression, excluding trailing spaces?
questions.title: Function returning character count excluding trailing spaces
questions.answer: LEN()

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **`LEN()`** (SQL Server) — it returns the length of a string excluding trailing spaces (unlike `DATALENGTH`, which counts raw bytes including trailing spaces).

UPDATE Employees SET Salary = Salary + 10 WHERE Department = 'Sales';
questions.answer: UPDATE Employees SET Salary = Salary * 1.10 WHERE Department = 'Sales';

sections.label: Answer

questions.question: Which grouping extension allows you to calculate grand totals and subtotals within a single query result alongside standard GROUP BY aggregates?
questions.title: Grouping extension for grand totals + subtotals in one query
questions.answer: ROLLUP

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **`ROLLUP`** (`GROUP BY ROLLUP(...)`) produces hierarchical subtotals plus a grand total alongside the normal grouped rows in a single result set.

questions.question: Which aggregate function is used to calculate the average value of a numeric column?
questions.title: Aggregate function for average value
questions.answer: AVG()

questions.question: What is the primary difference between the UNION and UNION ALL operators?
questions.title: UNION vs UNION ALL
options: UNION needs the same number of rows in both queries
UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them
UNION keeps duplicates; UNION ALL removes them
UNION ALL sorts the result; UNION does not
questions.answer: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: `UNION` **combines result sets and removes duplicate rows** (requiring an internal sort/distinct operation, which is costlier), while `UNION ALL` **combines result sets and keeps all rows including duplicates**, making it faster since no duplicate-elimination step is needed.

questions.question: Which database object stores the physical result set of a complex query and updates it periodically, improving read performance at the cost of storage space?
questions.title: Object storing a physical, periodically-refreshed result set
questions.answer: Materialized view

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Materialized View** — it physically stores the query's result set and refreshes it periodically (or on demand), trading extra storage for much faster read performance compared to re-computing the query (a regular/standard view) every time.

questions.question: In advanced SQL server architecture, what is the primary operational limitation imposed on a standard User-Defined Function (UDF) that fundamentally distinguishes it from the capabilities of a Stored Procedure?
questions.title: UDF limitation vs Stored Procedure
options: A UDF generally cannot modify database state (no DML or transaction control)
A UDF cannot be used inside SELECT statements
A UDF cannot return a value
questions.answer: A UDF generally cannot modify database state (no DML or transaction control)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A standard User-Defined Function **cannot perform actions that change database state — it cannot execute INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (DML) on tables or use transaction control statements (COMMIT/ROLLBACK), and it can typically only be used within expressions (like inside a SELECT)** — a Stored Procedure has no such restriction and can freely modify data and control transactions.

questions.title: Query to remove a 'Default' constraint (SQL Server)
options: ALTER TABLE TableName REMOVE DEFAULT ConstraintName;
ALTER TABLE TableName DROP CONSTRAINT ConstraintName;
questions.answer: ALTER TABLE TableName DROP CONSTRAINT ConstraintName;

sections.label: Answer
sections.content:
```sql
ALTER TABLE TableName DROP CONSTRAINT ConstraintName;
```
(where `ConstraintName` is the name of the DEFAULT constraint on that column).

questions.question: In pessimistic concurrency control modeling using the Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol, what specific operational guarantee does the protocol provide regarding the execution schedule of active concurrent database transactions?
questions.title: Strict Two-Phase Locking (2PL) — guarantee provided
options: It guarantees there are never any deadlocks
It guarantees conflict-serializable schedules (Strict 2PL also avoids cascading rollbacks)
It removes the need for commit
It runs transactions strictly in arrival order
questions.answer: It guarantees conflict-serializable schedules (Strict 2PL also avoids cascading rollbacks)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Strict 2PL guarantees that the resulting schedule is **conflict-serializable** (equivalent to some serial execution order of the transactions), and additionally (since it's the "strict" variant) it guarantees the schedule is **cascadeless**, since all exclusive locks are held until commit/abort.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a foreign key constraint?
questions.title: What is the purpose of a foreign key constraint?
options: To enforce referential integrity by linking a column to a primary key in another table
To speed up all SELECT queries automatically
To prevent a table from ever being deleted
questions.answer: To enforce referential integrity by linking a column to a primary key in another table

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Foreign keys are a core relational integrity constraint connecting related tables.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **A foreign key constraint ensures that a value in one table's column must exist as a valid primary/unique key value in another (referenced) table**, preventing orphaned records and maintaining referential integrity across relationships.

questions.question: What's the difference between a stored procedure and a user-defined function regarding return values?
questions.title: What's the difference between a stored procedure and a user-
options: A stored procedure can return zero, one, or multiple values/result sets; a scalar function must return exactly one value
Only functions can accept input parameters
Stored procedures cannot contain any SQL logic
Functions always run faster than stored procedures
questions.answer: A stored procedure can return zero, one, or multiple values/result sets; a scalar function must return exactly one value

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Both are reusable database objects but differ in usage context and return behavior.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **A stored procedure can return zero, one, or many result sets (or none at all) and can perform DML/transaction control, whereas a scalar user-defined function must always return exactly one value and is restricted from modifying database state**, making it usable directly inside expressions like SELECT statements.

questions.question: What does the SQL `HAVING` clause do that `WHERE` cannot?
questions.title: What does the SQL `HAVING` clause do that `WHERE` cannot?
options: HAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation
HAVING can only be used with SELECT *
WHERE can filter on aggregate functions directly
HAVING and WHERE are functionally identical
questions.answer: HAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: This relates to SQL's logical query processing order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping/aggregation happens, and cannot reference aggregate functions directly, while HAVING filters groups AFTER aggregation, and can filter based on aggregate results** (e.g., `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`).
